stories.title_en: Whatever became of holography? (2011)
stories.title_ja: ホログラフィーはどうなったのか？（2011）

comments.author: Nition
comments.text: I went to a whole art exhibition of holograms as a kid that blew me away, and I've always wondered why holograms are so rare ever since. I had one for a while, the famous one of the microsope with the lens that you can actually look through to see a computer chip inside. There's nothing else like it.

comments.author: daniel_reetz
comments.text: There's a phenomenal book on this topic called "Holographic Visions" (ISBN 978-0198571223). I've had the pleasure of working behind the scenes on holography related stuff (primarily optomechanics) for years now. Fascinating field full of phenomenally interesting minds.

comments.author: case540
comments.text: 3blue1brown’s video on holography is one of the coolest math videos I’ve ever seen. Basically magic.

comments.author: midnitewarrior
comments.text: I wanted to pick up doing holography again, but I discovered that Integraf, founded by legend TJ ( https://www.integraf.com/about/tung-h-jeong ), stopped selling the film and supplies. Much of the supply chain for modern hobbyist holography was sourced out of Russia, and the ongoing wars have made those materials unavailable. There are some newer processes out there, but there were probably thousands of us that grew up using those HoloKit holography kits distributed by TJ.

comments.author: zoeysmithe
comments.text: They always felt gimmicky to me, like something out of a kid's museum, and I imagine I'm not the only one. Its this odd often blurry and hard to see thing that certainly has interesting aspects but is not something you can create easily at home, unlike a photograph. Then the world changed and mobile devices ruled and everyone had a good camera sensor in their pocket, TVs were thinner and higher resolution than ever, games started looking amazing, etc and there really wasn't any room for less practical things like holograms. I think its one of those things we just weirdly romanticize like a car that is also a boat or a jetpack, but in reality has no real place as a consumer product.

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、ホログラフィーへのノスタルジーと芸術・教育的価値への関心と、ホビキット供給の断絶や製作の難しさ、さらにスマホや高解像度ディスプレイの普及により実用性が失われた点である。賛否両論については、賛成側は「魔法のような三次元像」、「知的刺激」、「アートとしての魅力」を挙げ、反対側は「製作が困難でブライヤー像が多い」、「高コストかつ供給が不安定」、「現代のデジタルメディアに比べて実用的でない」と指摘している。特に注目されたコメントは、インテグラフ創設者TJがフィルムとキットの販売を停止し、ロシア産サプライチェーンが戦争で途絶えたためホビーホログラフィーがほぼ不可能になったという指摘で、供給問題が現状の衰退の主因だと強調した点である。
stories.editor_note: ホログラフィーは2011年の記事だが、今AR/VRヘッドセット需要が高まり、ソニーやパナソニックが光学ホログラムディスプレイを開発中で、実用化への期待が再燃している。

stories.title_en: Governments are mishandling the affordability crisis

comments.author: taylortbb
comments.text: > They should lift incomes, not suppress prices I think this misses the psychology of inflation. If wages go up 20%, and prices go up 15%, everyone is better off and got a 5% raise, right? Go poll people that experienced that and they won't tell you they're celebrating being 5% richer, they'll tell you they're outraged about the 15% inflation. Psychologically they'll believe they earned that 20% raise through hard work. Putting in extra hours to get that promotion. But then the inflation robbed them of their 20% raise, and turned it into a measly 5% raise. They'll be outraged. Politicians get this. No one will credit politicians for raising average wages, people will believe they earned their raise themselves. But there's lots of votes available for lowering prices.

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、物価高騰への対策として政府が所得を引き上げるべきか、それとも価格を抑えるべきかという点。多くのコメントでは、賃金上昇でもインフレがそれを相殺すると実質的な利益が感じられず、有権者は自分で得た昇給だと考え、価格下落に感謝する心理があるため政治家は価格抑制に走ると指摘されている。一方で、政策決定者は危機から遠ざかっており問題を正しく対処できないという構造的批判や、再分配は左派政策であり最近の右派政権では実現しにくいという党派的視点、さらにインフレは隠れた税なので通貨供給の拡大を止め、支出を削減すべきという財政・金融論争も見られる。賛否は、所得引き上げを支持する意見と、価格抑制やインフレ抑制を優先すべき意見に分かれている。特に洞察にあるのは、賃金上昇が精神的に「自分の努力」だと感じられ、インフレがそれを奪うという心理論と、 insulated な政府が問題を悪化させるという指摘である。
stories.editor_note: 政府は負担能力危機を誤って扱っているという指摘は、物価高と賃金停滞が続く日本でも同様に、住宅・教育費の負担が若年層の消費を冷やし、内需回復の鍵となる政策転換が求められていることを示す。

stories.summary_ja: Beyond All Reason（BAR）はTotal Annihilationの精神的継承者として注目され、オープンソースでありながら洗練されたUIと豊富なQoL機能、さらに数万人規模の大規模戦闘が可能だと称賛されている。一方で、20年続くSpringエンジンやBalanced Annihilationプロジェクトとの違いが議論され、法的に独立させたBARが本当に優位か疑問視する声もある。また、Supreme Commanderのモホーエンジンを現代のツールで移植しようとする試みが挙げられ、64000機体の空戦を60fpsで動かすなど、性能面での大幅な向上が強調されている。Planetary Annihilationが元TA開発者による作品であることも触れられ、代替作品の多様性が指摘された。さらに、AI生成サイトを見分ける「01,02,03」番号のカードレイアウトについてのメタコメントが紹介された。

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、OpenStreetMap（OSM）を使って北朝鮮を詳細にマッピングしていることの意義と、その結果がもたらす情報へのアクセス向上についてだった。多くの参加者は、OSMがインターネットの「七不思議」の一つであると称賛し、データの見やすさやナビゲーションの快適さを挙げた。同時に、マッピングが逃走ルートの特定に使われる可能性について言及され、特に「P791」からの手紙が注目された。この手紙では、鳳西里周辺の細かいマッピングが逃走を助けるために行われていると書かれており、倫理的・人道的な側面が議論の焦点となった。賛否両論としては、マッピング自体への支持はほぼ全員一致だったが、記事中の図解を静止画として挿入すべきだという意見もあり、インタラクティブな形式よりも印刷物的な見やすさを求める声が上がった。また、観光客が自由に撮影したビデオがYouTubeに増えていることから、それらが北朝鮮の日常生活を垣間見る貴重な素材になっているというサイドコメントも共有された。注目コメントとしては、P791の手紙を「特に興味深い」と指摘し、マッピングが実際の人道支援や逃亡支援に直結していることを示した点が挙げられた。
stories.editor_note: 北朝鮮の測量士（2019）は、衛星画像解析が進む中で、国際機関が北朝鮮の軍事施設やミサイル基地を特定する手掛かりとして地元測量データに注目していることを示し、OSINTの重要性が高まっている。

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、指紋収集（フィンガープリント）がプライバシー侵害として既にEU法で禁止されており、同意バナーはクッキーそのものではなくトラッキング自体を規制する目的だという点。それに対し、技術的に興味深い一方でプライバシーへの恐怖を指摘する意見や、実際に導入を検討したがJA3/JA4 TLSフィンガープリントに切り替えた例も挙げられた。賛否は、指紋収集を「クールな技術」と肯定的に見る声と、根本的なプライバシー侵害だと批判する声に分かれ、防御手段の不足やTorブラウザーのみが有効だが使い勝ちが悪いという指摘もある。解決策として第三者広告の禁止を唯一の有効策だと主張する意見があり、一方でフェイクスローブラウザーや広告全面禁止といった猫と鼠の将来像を議論する声もある。特に注目されたのは、EUでの既存規制と同意バナーの真の目的を指摘したコメントと、第三者広告禁止を唯一の解決策だと断言した意見である。
stories.editor_note: 指紋は新しいクッキーだという主張は、ブラウザ指紋収集が広告ターゲティングに使われる現状を指し、日本でもプライバシー保護法改正が議論される中、指紋ベースのトラッキング規制の必要性が叫ばれている。

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、LLMの能力に対する共通認識のギャップが広がっていること。一部はプロンプトだけで複雑なプロジェクトが瞬時に完了すると楽観視し、開発スピードの向上を強調する。一方で、保守性・将来のトークンコスト・最適化の必要性・コードの劣化・LLMが生じがちな誤仮定への懸念から、人間によるコードレビューが不可欠だと主張する声が強い。さらに、一般ユーザーにとってAIは日常生活の利便性をほとんど向上させず、スマホ程度の機能しか求めていないため、エージェント型LLMへの関心は薄いという指摘がある。賛否は、技術者の間でのツール導入の是非と、実際に価値を生み出せるかへの懐疑に分かれる。注目コメントでは、「大規模プロジェクトがプロンプトで終わると思う0.2%は幻想で、保守レビューを不要とする派は将来的な不具合リスクを見過ごしている」と述べ、スピードと品質のトレードオフを警示した意見が挙げられた。
stories.editor_note: LLMの能力に関する共有理解のギャップが広がっているのは、企業が過大評価したAI導入で失敗例が増え、日本でも「AIリテラシー」向上のための社内研修が急務となっている背景を示す。

comments.author: dekhn
comments.text: I work in drug discovery and AI and his slide about cancer medicine isn't very well informed. We have models and narratives about how drugs work, but they are woefully incomplete. I ask nearly every doctor/researched in the medical field: if you had a AI-created drug that tremendously improved cancer treatment outcomes for your patient, would you hesitate to prescribe it because nobody understood how it worked? I have yet to hear "yes, I would hesitate", most people say "it would be cruel to deny a person a treatment that worked". I think Tao is focusing too much on second order effects of AI on math and other fields; humans are terrible at reasoning about second order effects, especially ones that are happening dynamically, in real time, using the most advanced mathematical models the world has yet created.

comments.author: squidmaster
comments.text: > Before injecting this cocktail into your bloodstream, would you want to know that there is at least one human cancer researcher who understands the mechanism behind this cure. Tao is out of his lane; lots of medicines don't have understood mechanisms. We don't even have the mechanisms behind general anesthesia nailed down; do you want to forgo it when the docs cut you open to remove your tumors?

comments.author: samuelknight
comments.text: Slide 12 and 13 sum up my conclusions from the Oct 8 100+ reactions to 100+ solutions. Several reported OpenAI drop included answers put a wrap on problems they had been working for years. Several said that they have to completely rewrite grant requests that they had just submitted. Others described learning of the solutions problems they had been working on like losing an old friend or a lover. The general sentiment was to bemoan the loss of a field, as if it would have been better be born in the early 20th century and conclude their career arc before reaching this point. My take away is that the field needs to get it through their heads that their old problems are no longer ambitious, and that their job in the short term is to find the new frontier. One idea Terrance Tao conjectures, which is highly doubtful, is that spamming the AI button will solve open problems without producing insightful new methods. But the OpenAI drop would seem to disprove this. The sub O(nlogn) proof for DFT for example violated very old human assumptions. Decades of work in the field was incremental progress on sub optimal method that nobody questioned hard enough. More generally, we should always be able to go back to a super-human AI and say, "Attack this problem, but don't use a method tried before."

comments.author: thomasahle
comments.text: Explaining Tao's point in software terms: the point of pure mathematics is to build and maintain a high quality "codebase" of theory, definitions and proofs. "Open problems are lighthouses not destinations" mean that these are currently not well explained by the theories and people should look into extending the codebase on that direction. The current generation of math AI is not a "good citizen" in that it doesn't try to make the most elegant additions to the shared framework, but will often just rebuild everything from scratch til get to some endpoint. Sure, we learned if the statement is true or false; but the proof can't be merged into the pure math codebase unless it's completely rebuilt. This is thankless work that humans are unlikely to want to do, and so the "solution" instead risks leaving a desolate patch of land, where existing efforts in extending the codebase lost their motivation. As with all things AI we can't take more than a 1-3 year horizon, if even that much. Probably AI will become better at respecting and working within the existing theories as it has with large software codebases.

comments.author: tripletao
comments.text: The bad cancer example is interesting to the extent it reveals that one of the world's top mathematicians is apparently unaware that applied science runs almost entirely on half-understood semi-empirical methods. That's most true for medicine, given the extreme complexity of human life; but if you look at a modern SPICE model for a transistor, a device that we claim to understand at the level of subatomic particles, then you'll find it's full of curve fits. As an engineer, I find that perfectly normal. My job is to use all the tools at my disposal to meet some human desire (to not die of exposure, for a slightly thinner phone, etc.), and whatever fundamental understanding I might have is only one tool to that end. My impression is that since pure mathematics doesn't attempt to meet those human desires they need some other objective, and that objective is human understanding. The loss of that is thus felt more heavily than in other fields. We could say it's their problem, and they need to get over it just like the chess players did; but the outside implications are broader here, since mathematicians working in fields they themselves considered useless have so frequently been wrong--in Hardy's Mathematician's Apology, he gave number theory as an example of such a field, unaware of what the cryptographers would achieve just decades later. It's possible that AI-generated pure math will continue this trend of delivering extraordinary unexpected societal value. It's also possible that the humans won't ever sufficiently understand that math, and the machines won't ever sufficiently understand human desires, and that connection won't be made. I've never met a pure mathematician who considered those downstream applications to be an important contributor to their motivations; but as AI-generated math contributes to the argument to allocate a large and increasing share of GDP to datacenter buildouts, that question of whether downstream value requires human understanding seems pressing.

stories.title_ja: パスキーは罠だ。使わないでください

comments.author: agwa
comments.text: Note that attestation can only be required during credential registration; at login time it's not possible to retroactively require attestation if it wasn't obtained during registration. And browsers will throw up a permission prompt if a website requests attestation. Are Netflix and Twitter currently requesting attestation when people register passkeys, and rejecting the registration if the user declines the permission prompt? I very much doubt it, since Apple's passkey implementation doesn't support attestation. Therefore, the author's scenario that sites will wait until most of their users are using attested passkeys and then "flip the switch and start rejecting non-attested passkeys" isn't very plausible. Attestation is certainly a stain on the WebAuthn spec, and it would have been better if Chrome and Firefox didn't support attestation (unless perhaps the browser is enrolled in enterprise management), but this blog post is presenting a hypothetical and unlikely scenario. That's not a good enough reason to recommend TOTP instead, given that TOTP is vulnerable to phishing and passkeys aren't. If consumer-facing sites start requesting attestation when registering passkeys, they deserve to be vigorously called out, and maybe then the recommendation to use passkeys should be revisited. But until that happens, don't tell people not to use passkeys.

comments.author: bmitch3020
comments.text: I've yet to voluntarily enable passkeys, for the main reason that I want portability, and not to be tied to any single device that can be lost. I want to be able to backup and lock my credentials in a safe. I also want to control the strength of my credentials for different services, and I don't consider my thumbprint used to unlock my phone to be as strong as a long password in a password manager. The first time I was forced to use a passkey implemented within the vendor's app (3rd party password managers were not an option). I quickly closed that account. The second time was an app that popped up a passkey opt-in in the middle of a bunch of transaction screens. I quickly realized the error, but there was no easy undo. The opt in was one green button in the middle of the screen. Turning it back off required digging through settings to find the security option to disable, and then confirm my choice multiple times. That process also signed out all my other devices. The fact that companies are resorting to dark patterns and forced requirements, where my money is held hostage, should be pretty good evidence of how poorly the passkey rollout is going.

comments.author: danpalmer
comments.text: The very last thing, past the conclusion, the very last footnote is: > Addendum: I feel I have made a compelling case for passkeys in this article. And I haven’t even pointed out one of their best security features: they are (in most use cases) domain-bound, meaning they are resistant to what are called Man-In-The-Middle attacks. "I made a compelling case... but didn't point out the most important security feature that motivated passkeys in the first place" Honestly I don't think this post did make a compelling case. There's a lot of assuming bad faith on the part of the FIDO alliance, while completely missing that preventing MITM attacks was a key design feature. The FIDO alliance members deal with stolen accounts all the time, and passkeys largely solve that. Stealing accounts is almost always done with phishing or social engineering, and passkeys solve the former and reduce the surface for the latter.

comments.author: david_shaw
comments.text: This is a (very long and) well-written treatise against passkeys in their common and disparate forms. It's worth reading, and brings up several interesting and often concerning points. I don't agree with the conclusion, though. TOTP is great, flexible, and keeps the user in control; however, using a passkey in a flexible password manager (Bitwarden, keepass, 1Password, etc) really does continue to give the user control. And the user experience is dramatically easier than filling in TOTP codes. To advocate for TOTP over passkeys, we're already relying on an application to generate those numbers (authenticator apps, password managers, etc). I see no reason to not simply continue using those pieces of software to manage passkeys, too.

comments.author: oefrha
comments.text: I’m an advocate for passkeys and I abolished passwords and embraced discoverable passkeys for our org’s key internal systems exclusively. So the battle cry of a title immediately put me on the defensive, unfortunately. The urge to not read is strong. A more measured title may help here. But there’s definitely a kernel of truth here. 1Password recently began to enforce userVerification: required[1][2], and suddenly on the desktop without TouchID I have to enter my login password to use the passkey on a good number of websites. I didn’t sign up for 1Password 15 years ago so that I have to enter both my very complex master password and very complex login password to sign into websites, the “one password” contract is suddenly broken after 15 years. This experience independently alarmed me about the additional constraints potential of the passkey standard and power wielded by the FIDO Alliance and partnering organizations addressed in TFA, which are, to be clear, useful for security in an organization. (We use userVerification: preferred now btw.) Therefore, I believe the passkey technology is great for enforcing a standard of security in an organization and stand by my choice for my org. But as a general purpose B2C auth tech, if the additional constraints become widely adopted, user freedom will be seriously harmed. Edit: I asked Opus 5.5 to vibe code a passkey auth solution in Go a few times without saying anything specific about userVerification. It chose required each time. So expect to see more of these. Oh and vibe coding auth without understanding it entirely is bad , please don’t do that. stories.summary_ja:
**主な議論点**  
- **アテステーションの問題**：アテステーションは登録時にしか要求できず、ブラウザは許可プロンプトを出すため、現在ほとんどのサイト（Netflix、Twitter等）はアテステーションを要求しておらず、将来的に「非アテステーションのパスキーを拒否するスイッチ」を切り替えるシナリオは現実的ではないという指摘。  
- **ポータビリティとバックアップ**：パスキーは特定デバイスに縛られがちで、バックアップや復元が難しいことが懸念された。ユーザーはパスワードマネージャーのように自由に移行・管理したいという意見が多い。  
- **ユーザー体験とダークパターン**：一部のアプリやサービスがパスキーのオプトインを強制的に表示し、オフにする手順が煩雑で、他のデバイスからサインアウトさせられるケースがあり、これが「ダークパターン」として批判された。  
- **ユーザーベリフィケーション（UV）の影響**：1Passwordなどが `userVerification: required` をデフォルトにし、デスクトップでTouchIDが無いときにログインパスワードを再入力させる仕様が、従来の「ひとつのパスワード」の利便性を損ねると指摘された。  
- **セキュリティの利点（MITM耐性）**：パスキーはドメインバインドのため、フィッシングや中間者攻撃に強いという点が再認識され、これを無視した批判は的外れだとする声もある。  

**賛否両論**  
- **賛成派**：パスキーはフィッシングに強く、組織内でのセキュリティ基準の統一に有用。パスワードマネージャーと組み合わせればポータビリティも確保できる。  
- **反対派**：現在の実装はデバイス縛りやUV強制によりユーザーの自由を奪い、ダークパターンが横行しているため、TOTPなど従来の方式の方が安全かつ使い勝手が良いと主張。  

**注目コメント**  
- 「アテステーションは登録時にしか要求できず、ブラウザが許可プロンプトを出すため、現在のサイトはほぼ要求していない。将来的に『スイッチを切り替える』シナリオは現実的ではない」という指摘は、議論の中心となる事実関係を明確にし、過度な懐疑論を抑える重要な意見として挙げられた。  
- また、あるユーザーは「1PasswordがUVを必須にしたことで、長年使ってきた『ひとつのパスワード』の利便性が失われた」と述べ、組織での利用は適切だが一般消費者向けには自由度が損なわれると警鐘を鳴らした。

comments.author: rkagerer
comments.text: I'll be tarred and feathered for saying this, but every time I see a modern chat app I pine for the days of ICQ (as it looked in the 90's). It had a UI I prefer over anything since - compact, comparatively unobtrusive, information-dense, and fast. I could port my full chat history around with me between machines, and also search it reliably (no vanishing scrolling or lazy-loading handicaps). And it was handy you could advertise different presence states to different people/groups.

comments.author: theshrike79
comments.text: As someone who's still on IRC daily and has built multiple IRC bots and clients over the years: - most of the jank of IRC is client-side and can be fixed on the clients, IRCv3 protocol changes are nice, but not essential for a good experience. - bots can make channels more engaging, just posting the titles of URLs pasted on the channels so even people without fancy rich clients can see what's behind a YouTube link or Reddit share url without clicking it open makes the experience more "discord/slack-like" - IRC bots and clients are super fun and easy first projects for any language, you get to do permanently open sockets to multiple destinations (multi-server of course), asynchronous stuff and text handling. I went with IRCCloud for the longest time myself until early this year, due to the November Revolution of AI models getting super good, I figured out I can build my own IRCCloud just the way I like it with the price of a single Claude Pro subscription. And so I did. I think I had an MVP running in a week (evenings on my free time) and over the summer I cancelled my IRCCloud subscription and I'm fully using my own system. comments.author: brandonpelfrey
comments.text: Unless you explicitly need byte-matching decompilation, there are significantly faster ways to produce a decompilation/C which is functionally equivalent. I need to post about this. What's been working for me is that for every function, Agent A is tasked with writing some code which is semantically equivalent to the original assembly, but not necessarily exactly the same. Agent A also writes tests. Agent A submits the implementation of the function and tests to the harness for it to judge. The harness runs both the original function and the submitted function in a virtual machine/simulator/emulator (the tests define function inputs and starting state). The harness will only accept the implementation if 1) the read/write sequence to RAM is identical to the original function's, and 2) there must be complete line and branch coverage of the original function being decompiled. I've found this to be robust for decompiling games, while giving the agents enough freedom to write code that is readable and not waste a ton of time making sure e.g. instruction ordering, register assignments, etc. are all exactly the same. For me, having byte-matching decompilation is only one way to produce a decompilation I know is faithful to the original. This "high-level decompilation" process I just described is something agents can do much more quickly.

comments.text: The reason this cost so much is because the AI has the ridiculous goal of getting identical assembly output. The agents would have had to mess around with compiler versions, optimisation options, and the phase of the moon as well. If you just went for functional equivalence, it would probably cost 10x or 100x less tokens. Another false economy was using Sonnet instead of a more intelligent model like Sol 6.1 (1), which would have cost more per token, but is 100x or so better at reverse engineering and coding and therefore can chew through the source code much quicker and make fewer mistakes, meaning less work needing to be scrapped. In my testing doing a similar task, I ran multiple sonnet for weeks and burnt through ~$1000 in tokens to get 20% completion and output that was pretty bad. After switching to Sol 6.1, it finished the whole task in around 2 days, cost around $50, and it did it with zero supervision and a single /goal. (1): struggle to use Opus for reverse engineering, too many safeguards. OAI has virtually none, and uses way less tokens so is more economical.

comments.author: cagster
comments.text: I wrote plimsoll for my own projects. Several have an agent writing and running code, and they all needed the same things: a way for that code to call my APIs without holding a credential, a record of exactly what ran with checksums I can verify, and a way to tie each run to my own logs. I also wanted one place to use several sandboxes, local or cloud, so I can test on my machine and flip a switch for production. Plimsoll is a Go daemon you run yourself, and the switch is its configuration: WebAssembly or plain docker on a laptop; docker under gVisor, or E2B and Docker Cloud microVMs, in production. The client code doesn't change. Every result states its isolation tier (process, container, kernel or vm), and a request can set a minimum, so code that needs a VM can't quietly run on my test setup: below the floor, nothing runs. E2B and Docker Cloud bill by the second and agents never get bored, so each caller can get a daily allowance of microVM seconds. An agent that wants to loop forever loops until the allowance runs out; the next run is refused before it starts. Sessions keep one sandbox across calls, with Python or JavaScript cells that keep their state like a notebook (on docker, E2B and NVIDIA's OpenShell). Every response carries a run record, SHA-256 hashes of the request and result that the clients recompute; in a session the records chain, and a separate tool, plimsoll-attest, signs them and refuses a chain with a call missing. Pass your own trace ID and it lands on the daemon's audit line. The code gets no network by default. To call one of my APIs it goes through a broker outside the sandbox: the run's grant lists the exact routes allowed, and the broker adds a token minted for that run, which never enters the sandbox, and enforces call and size budgets. It traces each call by the route pattern it matched (/items/*, not /items/42), status, size and timing, never the body or token; the audit line gets the totals, and an optional advisor flags waste, like an agent fetching 200 items one at a time, which is the most agent thing an agent can do. To try it you only need Go (process tier, so not for hostile code): git clone https://github.com/plimsollmark/plimsoll && cd plimsoll go run ./examples/minimal On Linux with docker, the same example at the kernel tier: sudo ./docker/install-gvisor.sh && make docker-images SANDBOX_PROVIDER=docker SANDBOX_DOCKER_RUNTIME=runsc go run ./examples/minimal Clients: Go, Python (tools for Agno, CrewAI and Google ADK) and TypeScript (Vercel AI SDK, Trigger.dev, Mastra). What it isn't yet: pre-1.0, no other users, no outside security audit, and it's just me: the bus factor is one, and I'm careful around buses. gVisor is Linux only, so a Mac gets the container tier. The tier is configuration plus startup smoke tests, not attestation. If you run agent-written code today, what do you run it in? Would a tier label change what you trust?

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点は、Plimsoll が提供するセルフホスト型サンドボックスの設計と、既存のリモートサンドボックス（exe.dev）との違いである。コメントでは、Plimsoll の構成可能な隔離レベル（プロセス、コンテナー、gVisor カーネル、VM、E2B/Docker Cloud マイクロVM）と、各ランの認証トークンをサンドボックス外のブローカーが付与する仕組み、実行記録の SHA‑256 チェックサムとチェーン、セッション状態の保持、使用量ベースのマイクロVM秒数割り当てなどが詳しく説明されている。また、デフォルトでネットワーク遮断、API 呼び出しのルートベースのトレースと予算 enforce、トレース ID の付与による監査ログ連携も特徴として挙げられている。

賛否両論については、肯定的な側面として「自前でホストできるためトークン漏洩リスクが低い」「隔離レベルを設定・切替え可能でテストと本番を同じクライアントコードで扱える」「実行記録の改ざん防止とセッション状態の保存が便利」という点が挙げられている。一方、懸念点として「プレリリース段階で外部セキュリティ監査がない」「開発者が一人だけ（バスファクター=1）」「gVisor が Linux 限定で macOS ではコンテナーレベルに落ちる」「まだユーザーベースが小さい」などが指摘されている。

注目コメントとして、作者自身が「自分のプロジェクトでエージェントが書いたコードを安全に実行するために必要だった機能（API コールのためのクレデンシャルレスブローカー、実行チェックサム、ログ連携、複数サンドボックスへの切替えスイッチ）をすべて一つの Go デーモンにまとめた」という説明が挙げられ、これが Plimsoll の設計動機と実用性を如実に示している。さらに、プレビュー試し方として「Go だけでプロセスレベルの実行が可能」かつ「Linux+gVisor でカーネルレベル、本番では E2B/Docker Cloud のマイクロVMに切替え可能」という具体的な手順が紹介されている。以上が議論の要点である。
stories.editor_note: Show HN: Plimsoll、AIエージェントが書くコードのためのセルフホストドサンドボックスは、AI生成コードのセキュリティ検証が急務となり、日本の金融機関でもサンドボックス導入を進め、生成AIの実務利用におけるリスク低減を図っている動きと合致する。

comments.author: crazygringo
comments.text: I think we're about to see a dictation revolution. I've been coding with Claude, and I pretty much do it exclusively by voice now, simply because it's so much faster. And I kind of feel like Scotty from Star Trek IV, when he holds up a Mac mouse to try to talk into it. I've been using VoiceInk [1] which looks like it's basically the same as this, but has been around for longer. What has really made it work for me is using a Bluetooth media control like [2], where I use Karabiner Elements to remap its play/pause button to the dictation keyboard shortcut. I map rewind to option-backspace to delete the last word, fast-forward to shift-enter to insert a newline, a lower button to enter to submit my prompt, and the volume up/down buttons to scroll up/down. I've also just ordered to Xiaomi Bluetooth remote [3] that includes a microphone itself to see if I can get it to work by speaking directly into it and using it as the microphone -- there are a couple of open source projects to turn it into a Mac microphone directly. Since I'd like to be able to talk more quietly instead of into my Mac. But what I'm REALLY waiting for is the ability to use one button for dictation, and a second button for issuing commands for a local LLM to interpret. So I hold down the voice button which transcribes "I think we need to catch that" and then the second button and go "change catch to cache, like c-a-c-h-e". Or hold down the second button and go "switch to VS code". I don't want something as finicky as macOS Voice Control, I want a local LLM I can speak naturally to. I can very much see a future where I spend the majority of my "work" time using a Apple TV-type remote. [1] https://github.com/Beingpax/VoiceInk [2] https://www.amazon.com/Satechi-Bluetooth-Multimedia-Remote-C... [3] https://www.notebookcheck.net/Xiaomi-Bluetooth-Remote-2-Pro-...
